fixes.explanation: That's right, friend. Paul says, "…after I have completed this service and have safely delivered this bounty to them, I will set off to Spain by way of you." (Romans 15:28) So the delivery in Jerusalem comes first. After that he sets off for Spain by way of Rome.

Paul says they're "…able to instruct one another." (Romans 15:14) He isn't just patting them on the head. He's saying the believers in Rome can teach each other. Friend, that's a compliment with some weight on it.
An invitation is what I send out for a cookie night, but that's not the word Paul picks. He says "…a bold reminder on some points…" (Romans 15:15) He's bringing back to mind what they already know.
The verse doesn't say anyone in Rome asked. Paul gives his reason himself: "…because of the grace God has given me" (Romans 15:15) The text points to God's grace, not a request from the church.
This passage never says Paul started that church. His reason is "…because of the grace God has given me" (Romans 15:15) The text gives grace as the reason, and that's the answer here.

Sounds like a trick, friend, but this one is true. Paul says the Gentiles become an offering "…sanctified by the Holy Spirit." (Romans 15:16) Sanctified means made holy. The Holy Spirit gets the credit for that holy part.

This verse isn't about the other apostles. Paul says he'll speak only of "…what Christ has accomplished through me…" (Romans 15:18) He's talking about his own work among the Gentiles, and every bit of the credit goes to Christ. Honestly, I'd be tempted to sneak a little "me" in there.

That's a comfortable place to work, but Paul says something different. He aspired to preach "…where Christ was not known…" (Romans 15:20) That's where he's aiming, and strong churches aren't his target here.

Paul never mentions his family in this passage. He says he aspired to preach the gospel "…where Christ was not known…" (Romans 15:20) His aim is about places where Christ was not known, not about who lives down the street. Friend, I'd pack a cookie box for a trip like that.

Careful, friend. Paul quotes Isaiah, and the line says the opposite: "Those who were not told about Him will see, and those who have not heard will understand." (Romans 15:21) So the ones who were never told DO get to see. Paul brings it in right after saying he aspired to preach where Christ was not known.

Right on the money. Paul quotes, "Those who were not told about Him will see, and those who have not heard will understand." (Romans 15:21) People who were never told will see and understand. Paul brings it in right after saying he aspired to preach where Christ was not known.

Paul says the opposite. He writes that "…there are no further opportunities for me in these regions…" (Romans 15:23) That comes right after he says he has fully proclaimed the gospel from Jerusalem to Illyricum. Then he turns to his long wish to visit Rome.

Arabia doesn't show up in Paul's plan in this passage. He says, "I hope to see you on my way to Spain." (Romans 15:24) Spain is the destination, and Rome is on the route. Good guess, but the compass points somewhere else.

Jerusalem makes the temple spring to mind, friend, so I see why priests came up. But the verse doesn't send the gift to them. It says the contribution is "…for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem." (Romans 15:26) The saints are the believers there, and the gift is for the ones in need.

Gentiles is a word that shows up in this passage, but not in this request. Paul asks to be delivered from "…the unbelievers in Judea…" (Romans 15:31) The word that fits the first blank is unbelievers.
Hidden isn't a word in Paul's request. He asks that his service in Jerusalem "…may be acceptable to the saints there…" (Romans 15:31) Acceptable is the word that fits the blank.
